pool.title: Thailand eliminates rubella as a public health problem, WHO says
pool.summary: The World Health Organization verified that Thailand has eliminated endemic rubella—the seventh country in WHO’s South-East Asia Region to do so. Years of childhood immunization and careful disease tracking helped protect families from congenital rubella syndrome.
pool.summaryLong:
The World Health Organization today announced that Thailand has been verified for eliminating rubella as a public health problem, marking a major milestone in the country’s efforts to protect children, women and families from vaccine-preventable diseases.

Rubella, also known as German measles, is a contagious viral infection. Rubella infection during pregnancy can cause miscarriage, stillbirth or congenital rubella syndrome, a condition associated with lifelong birth defects. Rubella can be prevented through safe, effective and affordable vaccines.

“Thailand has shown that rubella elimination is achievable when strong political commitment, resilient immunization services, high-quality surveillance and community trust come together. This achievement protects future generations from congenital rubella syndrome and brings the Region closer to eliminating both measles and rubella,” said Dr Nilesh Buddha, Officer-in-Charge, WHO South-East Asia Region, endorsing the recommendation of the Regional Verification Commission for Measles and Rubella Elimination in the South-East Asia Region (SEA-RVC).

The SEA-RVC, which held its annual meeting from 22–23 June 2026, reviewed evidence submitted by Thailand’s National Verification Committee, including data on disease surveillance, molecular epidemiology, immunization coverage, outbreak response and programme performance. This was followed by a verification field visit in July 2026 and the Commission recommended that Thailand be verified for endemic rubella elimination.

Thailand is now the seventh country in the WHO South-East Asia Region to achieve rubella elimination, joining Bhutan, DPR Korea, Maldives, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Timor-Leste. Four countries in the Region - Bhutan, DPR Korea, Maldives and Timor-Leste - have eliminated both measles and rubella.

Verification confirms that Thailand has met the requisite criteria for interruption of endemic rubella virus transmission and has systems in place to sustain this achievement.

pool.title: NASA’s Prithvi becomes the first AI geospatial model flown in orbit
pool.summary: Researchers uploaded NASA and IBM’s open-source Prithvi model to a satellite and an ISS payload, testing flood and cloud detection from space. Sharing the model openly meant the team did not have to train a foundation model from scratch.
pool.summaryLong:
A team from Adelaide University, ESA Φ-lab, Thales Alenia Space, and SmartSat CRC demonstrated NASA and IBM’s open-source Prithvi Geospatial AI foundation model aboard two in-orbit platforms—the South Australian government’s Kanyini satellite and the Thales Alenia Space IMAGIN-e payload on the International Space Station. That makes Prithvi the first geospatial foundation model deployed in orbit.

Trained on about 13 years of Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 data, Prithvi can be adapted for tasks such as mapping flood plains, monitoring disasters, and predicting crop yields. In the demo, researchers tested flood and cloud detection across two different orbiting platforms and computing environments.

Foundation models are pre-trained on vast unlabeled datasets, then fine-tuned for specific jobs with far less labeled data. Active satellites often cannot accept large software updates, so onboard AI tends to be lightweight and specialized. With a foundation model architecture, operators can add a small decoder package for a new task instead of uploading an entirely new model—saving precious bandwidth.

“If Prithvi weren’t open source, I would have to train my own foundation model,” said lead researcher Dr. Andrew Du of Adelaide University and SmartSat CRC. “Having that model openly available saved a lot of time and effort.”

Kevin Murphy, NASA’s chief science data officer, said putting Prithvi in orbit shows why the agency shares AI tools: “By sharing these tools with anyone who wants to use them, we accelerate scientific and technological development into the future.” NASA’s IMPACT AI team at Marshall Space Flight Center co-developed Prithvi with IBM. Related open models include the heliophysics model Surya, released in 2025.

On Feb. 20, 2026, the Galápagos National Park Directorate and partners released 158 giant tortoises at two sites on Floreana Island—the first wild return of the island’s tortoises in more than 150 years. Hunting and introduced predators wiped them out in the mid-1800s; without them, the island’s vegetation and seed pathways changed.

NASA Earth observations help answer a practical question: where the animals have the best chance to survive not just today, but decades from now. Landsat and Sentinel track vegetation; the Global Precipitation Measurement mission supplies rainfall; Terra estimates land-surface temperature; terrain data adds elevation. A decision tool combines those measurements with millions of field observations of tortoise locations across the archipelago.

“This is exactly the kind of project where NASA Earth observations make a difference,” said Keith Gaddis of NASA Earth Action’s Biological Diversity and Ecological Forecasting program. James Gibbs of Galápagos Conservancy noted Charles Darwin was among the last people to see tortoises there. DNA work linking living tortoises on Isabela’s Wolf Volcano to extinct Floreana ancestry helped launch a breeding program that produced animals for return.

The release is part of the larger Floreana Ecological Restoration Project, which aims to remove invasive rats and feral cats and eventually restore 12 native species, with tortoises as a keystone. Because tortoises can live more than a century, forecasting habitat decades ahead matters as much as today’s conditions.

pool.title: NOAA funds a system-wide restoration push for Florida’s Indian River Lagoon

The lagoon once held expansive seagrass beds and clear water. Pollution, habitat loss, and harmful algal blooms took a heavy toll; between 2011 and 2020, blooms killed an estimated 89 percent of the seagrass. A recent study cited in NOAA’s feature found the lagoon generates $28.3 billion in local economic activity each year and supports 128,400 jobs.

“This project brings together scientists, managers, and community members across the entire lagoon to focus on the places and actions most likely to make a system-wide difference,” said NOAA Marine Habitat Resource Specialist Erin McDevitt. Council Executive Director Duane De Freese said the NOAA funding made the broad coalition possible. Some NOAA-funded projects are already complete; others run through 2027, with extra support to measure how the ecosystem responds over time.

pool.title: NOAA’s wave-exposure model returns as free open-source R software
pool.summary: NCCOS re-released WEMo as an R package so coastal managers can estimate wind-driven wave height and energy without proprietary GIS lock-in. The tool has already guided seagrass restoration and living-shoreline design.
pool.summaryLong:
Researchers at NOAA’s National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science re-released the Wave Exposure Model (WEMo) as a free, open-source R package. The modernized tool estimates wind-driven wave height and energy in coastal environments—helping identify shoreline vulnerability and erosion hot spots so restoration dollars go where they help most.

Physical wave sensors are expensive and cover only a few spots. WEMo instead uses mathematical modeling with NOAA meteorological observations, underwater topography, and shoreline shape to simulate wave energy across larger areas from a desk. It is designed for people with basic GIS knowledge, not only hydrodynamics specialists.

Originally released in 2006 as a proprietary ArcMap extension, the new R version adds easier access to NOAA input data, efficient re-analysis, modern visualization, and tutorials. To date, WEMo has supported seagrass restoration, living-shoreline design, and coastal management options. The work is supported by the Coastal Zone Management Act.

The Sihek was last seen in the wild on Guam in 1988 and is classified extinct in the wild; only about 143 birds remain across 23 facilities. Brown tree snakes introduced to Guam devastated native birds. The last 29 wild Sihek entered human care in the mid-1980s to start a breeding program.

Nine Sihek moved to Palmyra in 2024 have survived, established territories, and begun nesting. The atoll is free of snakes and rats; The Nature Conservancy and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service share stewardship there. “We’re honored to have been trusted with Guafi’s care these past few years and overjoyed that he may soon be flying free on Palmyra,” said Nicole LaGreco of the Oregon Zoo. Hugging Face has become a public square for open AI model cards, including science models developed with NASA and IBM. Visitors can read documentation, try demos where available, and follow links to GitHub code without buying a commercial API.

Hosting foundation models for Earth and planetary science on a free platform means a graduate student in Oregon and a nonprofit abroad can start from the same checkpoint. Clear licenses and community discussion reduce friction that used to keep research models inside a single lab. It is useful tech infrastructure with an open door.
